answer.short:
$a=b=c=d$.

Rearrangement gives $(a-b)^2+(b-c)^2+(c-d)^2=0$, so each square is zero.
answer.worked:
From the given equality,
$$\begin{align*}0&=(a+b)^2+(b+c)^2+(c+d)^2-4(ab+bc+cd)\\0&=a^2+2ab+b^2+b^2+2bc+c^2+c^2+2cd+d^2-4ab-4bc-4cd\\0&=a^2-2ab+b^2+b^2-2bc+c^2+c^2-2cd+d^2\\0&=(a-b)^2+(b-c)^2+(c-d)^2.\end{align*}$$
Each square is non-negative, so their sum is zero only when all three are zero. Thus $a-b=0$, $b-c=0$ and $c-d=0$, giving $a=b=c=d$.

$$\begin{align*}3a^2+4b^2+18c^2-4ab-12ac&=(a^2-4ab+4b^2)+2(a^2-6ac+9c^2)\\3a^2+4b^2+18c^2-4ab-12ac&=(a-2b)^2+2(a-3c)^2.\end{align*}$$

answer.worked:
Simplify the first operand using a common denominator.

$$\begin{align*}2-\frac{3n}{m}+\frac{9n^2-2m^2}{m^2+2mn}&=\frac{2m(m+2n)-3n(m+2n)+9n^2-2m^2}{m(m+2n)}\\2-\frac{3n}{m}+\frac{9n^2-2m^2}{m^2+2mn}&=\frac{mn+3n^2}{m(m+2n)}\\2-\frac{3n}{m}+\frac{9n^2-2m^2}{m^2+2mn}&=\frac{n(m+3n)}{m(m+2n)}\end{align*}$$

Clear the fraction in the nested denominator.

$$\begin{align*}m-2n-\frac{4n^2}{m+n}&=\frac{(m-2n)(m+n)-4n^2}{m+n}\\m-2n-\frac{4n^2}{m+n}&=\frac{m^2-mn-6n^2}{m+n}\\m-2n-\frac{4n^2}{m+n}&=\frac{(m-3n)(m+2n)}{m+n}\end{align*}$$

Then simplify the divisor.

$$\begin{align*}\frac1m-\frac{1}{m-2n-\frac{4n^2}{m+n}}&=\frac1m-\frac{m+n}{(m-3n)(m+2n)}\\\frac1m-\frac{1}{m-2n-\frac{4n^2}{m+n}}&=\frac{(m-3n)(m+2n)-m(m+n)}{m(m-3n)(m+2n)}\\\frac1m-\frac{1}{m-2n-\frac{4n^2}{m+n}}&=\frac{-2n(m+3n)}{m(m-3n)(m+2n)}\end{align*}$$

Multiply by the reciprocal and cancel common factors.

$$\begin{align*}\left(2-\frac{3n}{m}+\frac{9n^2-2m^2}{m^2+2mn}\right)\div\left(\frac1m-\frac{1}{m-2n-\frac{4n^2}{m+n}}\right)&=\frac{n(m+3n)}{m(m+2n)}\times\frac{m(m-3n)(m+2n)}{-2n(m+3n)}\\\left(2-\frac{3n}{m}+\frac{9n^2-2m^2}{m^2+2mn}\right)\div\left(\frac1m-\frac{1}{m-2n-\frac{4n^2}{m+n}}\right)&=\frac{3n-m}{2}\end{align*}$$

Clear the fractions in each compound fraction and factorise.

$$\begin{align*}\frac{1}{x+\frac{1}{x+2}}&=\frac{x+2}{x(x+2)+1}\\\frac{1}{x+\frac{1}{x+2}}&=\frac{x+2}{(x+1)^2}\\\frac{1}{x+\frac{1}{x-2}}&=\frac{x-2}{x(x-2)+1}\\\frac{1}{x+\frac{1}{x-2}}&=\frac{x-2}{(x-1)^2}\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}\frac{x-\frac4x}{x^2-2+\frac{1}{x^2}}&=\frac{x^3-4x}{x^4-2x^2+1}\\\frac{x-\frac4x}{x^2-2+\frac{1}{x^2}}&=\frac{x(x-2)(x+2)}{(x-1)^2(x+1)^2}\end{align*}$$

Multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor.

$$\begin{align*}\frac{1}{x+\frac{1}{x+2}}\times\frac{1}{x+\frac{1}{x-2}}\div\frac{x-\frac4x}{x^2-2+\frac{1}{x^2}}&=\frac{x+2}{(x+1)^2}\times\frac{x-2}{(x-1)^2}\times\frac{(x-1)^2(x+1)^2}{x(x-2)(x+2)}\\\frac{1}{x+\frac{1}{x+2}}\times\frac{1}{x+\frac{1}{x-2}}\div\frac{x-\frac4x}{x^2-2+\frac{1}{x^2}}&=\frac1x\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: Find $x$ in terms of $a$ and $b$ if $\dfrac{a^2b}{x^2}+\left(1+\dfrac{b}{x}\right)a=2b+\dfrac{a^2}{x}$.

answer.short:
Take the nonzero values among $x=a$ and $x=\dfrac{ab}{a-2b}$; the second expression applies when $a\ne2b$.

If $a=b=0$, every $x\ne0$ is a solution. If $a=0$ and $b\ne0$, there is no solution.

Multiply by $x^2$ and factorise.
answer.worked:
The original equation requires $x\ne0$. Multiplying by $x^2$ gives
$$\begin{align*}a^2b+ax^2+abx&=2bx^2+a^2x\\(a-2b)x^2+(ab-a^2)x+a^2b&=0\\(x-a)\bigl((a-2b)x-ab\bigr)&=0.\end{align*}$$
Thus $x=a$ is a solution when $a\ne0$. When $a\ne2b$, the other candidate is
$$\begin{align*}(a-2b)x&=ab\\x&=\frac{ab}{a-2b},\end{align*}$$
and it is retained only if it is nonzero.

If $a=2b\ne0$, the second factor is the nonzero constant $-ab$, so $x=a$ is the only solution. If $a=b=0$, the original equation is $0=0$ for every $x\ne0$. If $a=0$ and $b\ne0$, it becomes $0=2b$, so there is no solution.

entries.description:
Fluency in algebra, particularly in factoring, is absolutely vital for everything in mathematics. This chapter is intended as a review of earlier algebraic techniques, and readers should do as much or as little of it as necessary. Some readers will work steadily through it. Others will remember that this review is here, and work through parts of it as necessary.

The course properly begins with Chapter 2.

The word ‘algebra’ has an interesting history. Al-Khwarizmi was a famous and influential Persian mathematician who worked in Baghdad during the early ninth century when the Baghdad Caliphate excelled in science and mathematics. The Arabic word ‘algebra’ comes from al-jabr, a word in the title of his most important work, and means ‘the restoration of broken parts’ — a reference to the balancing of terms on both sides of an equation. Al-Khwarizmi’s own name came into modern European languages as ‘algorithm’.

entries.description:
This chapter reviews the manipulation of algebraic expressions involving pronumerals, where a pronumeral is a letter or symbol that stands ‘for a number’. The pronumeral may stand for a known or unknown constant, or for an unknown number in an equation, or it may be a variable and stand for any one of a whole set of possible numbers.

Pronumerals are numbers, so they can take part in all the normal operations of arithmetic, including addition, subtraction, multiplication, division (except by zero), and forming powers.

entries.sourceLabel: Algebraic expressions — like and unlike terms
entries.description:
An algebraic expression consists of pronumerals, numbers, and the operations of arithmetic. Here an algebraic expression is simplified by collecting like terms:
\(x^2+2xy+3x^2-4xy-3=4x^2-2xy-3\)
This particular algebraic expression can be simplified by combining like terms.
• The two like terms \(x^2\) and \(3x^2\) can be combined to give \(4x^2\).
• Another pair of like terms \(2xy\) and \(-4xy\) can be combined to give \(-2xy\).
• This yields three unlike terms, \(4x^2\), \(-2xy\) and \(-3\), which cannot be combined.
Assuming that these very basic foundations are well known, we now begin reviewing further methods that have been developed to handle algebraic expressions.

entries.description: Recognising quadratics that are perfect squares. A quadratic is called a perfect square if it is the square of a binomial expression. The special expansions in Section 1A gave the perfect square formula in two forms: Square of a sum: A² + 2AB + B² = (A + B)². Square of a difference: A² − 2AB + B² = (A − B)². Where we have reversed the sides to make them into identities for factoring: x² + 6x + 9 = (x + 3)² and x² − 18xy + 81y² = (x − 9y)². There is a test to check if x² + 6x + 9 is a perfect square: Halve the coefficient 6 of x to get 3, then square it to get 9. Because 9 is the constant term, this means it is a perfect square. The previous method of factoring a quadratic will still work, but recognising perfect squares is quicker, and is an important skill in itself. We will look again at perfect squares in Section 1D.
